1.1.title: Ledger Basics: Invoice Lines
1.1.quest: Implement format_invoice(invoice_id, amount, paid). Return exactly "<id> | <amount to 2 decimals> USD | PAID" (or UNPAID when paid is False). Do not print instead of returning. Example: format_invoice("INV-1001", 1234.5, True) → "INV-1001 | 1234.50 USD | PAID". Accept negative and zero amounts (credit notes are negative).
hints: Start with status = "PAID" if paid else "UNPAID".
Use an f-string with {amount:.2f}; spaces and punctuation are part of the contract.

0.title: Variables are labels
body: A **variable** is a name attached to a value — like a label on a spreadsheet cell. You create one with `=`.
Once a name exists you can reuse it anywhere below that line. Python reads your file from top to bottom.
0.code:
amount = 1234.5
invoice = "INV-1001"
paid = True
print(invoice, amount, paid)
0.note: `=` stores a value. `==` asks a question ("are these equal?"). Mixing them up is the most common beginner bug.

1.title: Four basic types
body: Every value has a **type**. You will use these four constantly:
`int` — whole numbers like `42`. `float` — decimals like `3.3`. `str` — text in quotes like `"INV-1001"`. `bool` — `True` or `False`.
Quotes matter: `"3.3"` is text, `3.3` is a number. `type(x)` tells you what you have.

3.title: Functions are reusable formulas
body: A **function** packages a piece of logic so you can reuse it. Parameters are the inputs you hand in; `return` is the answer you get back, like a spreadsheet formula.
The body is everything indented by four spaces under the `def` line. The function does nothing until you **call** it with parentheses.
3.code:
def double(x):
    result = x * 2
    return result

print(double(21))

6.title: Formatting numbers with f-strings
body: Put `f` before a string and you can drop values into it with `{}`.
After a colon you can add a **format spec**. `:.2f` means "show as a float with exactly 2 decimal places" — it rounds the display and leaves the original value alone.
6.code:
amount = 19.999
print(f"Total = {amount:.2f} USD")
print(f"Total = {0:.2f} USD")
print(amount)

7.title: Picking between two values
body: A **conditional expression** chooses one of two values in a single line: `A if condition else B`.
It is perfect for turning a bool into a label.
7.code:
paid = False
status = "PAID" if paid else "UNPAID"
print(status)

8.explain: :.2f always shows exactly two decimals, padding with zeros when needed.

9.title: Your mission: format_invoice
body: You will write `format_invoice(invoice_id, amount, paid)` and **return** one line of text. The exact shape is `<id> | <amount with 2 decimals> USD | PAID` — or `UNPAID` when `paid` is False. Every space and `|` counts.

Examples the tests will check: `format_invoice("INV-1001", 1234.5, True)` → `"INV-1001 | 1234.50 USD | PAID"` and `format_invoice("INV-0", 0, False)` → `"INV-0 | 0.00 USD | UNPAID"`. Negative amounts (credit notes) work the same way.
9.note: Next: a 3-question quiz on these ideas. Pass it and the Build step unlocks.

0.explanation: An f-string evaluates amount and :.2f displays exactly two decimal places.

1.2.title: Price Check: Loops & Lists
1.2.quest: Implement filter_prices(prices, low, high). Return a new list containing prices in the inclusive [low, high] range, in original order. Never mutate prices. Raise ValueError when low > high.
hints: Check low > high before the loop, even when prices is empty.
Create result = []; append only prices satisfying low <= price <= high.

0.title: Lists hold prices in order
body: A **list** is an ordered column of figures: `[10, 20, 30]`. Each item has an index, and indexing starts at **0**.
Negative indexes count from the end: `-1` is the last item. `len(prices)` gives the item count.

3.title: Conditions decide what passes
body: `if` runs its body only when the condition is True. Comparisons like `<`, `<=`, `==` produce bools.
Python lets you **chain** comparisons: `low <= x <= high` means "x is between low and high, including both ends" — like asking whether a price falls inside a budget range.

4.title: Build a new list, keep the input intact
body: To filter, start with an empty list and `append` what you want to keep. The caller's original list stays unchanged.
Never delete items from a list while looping over it — the loop skips elements and the caller gets a surprise.

8.title: Your mission: filter_prices
body: Write `filter_prices(prices, low, high)` returning a **new** list of prices where `low <= price <= high`, in the original order. Don't modify `prices`. If `low > high`, raise `ValueError`. Example: `filter_prices([-3, 0, 2, 5, 8], 0, 5)` → `[0, 2, 5]`. An empty input returns `[]`.

0.title: Dictionaries map names to values
body: A **dict** stores key → value pairs, like a spreadsheet row with a named column for each fact. Look a value up with `d[key]`.
A missing key raises `KeyError`. `d.get(key, default)` returns the default instead.

0.title: Virtual environments
body: A **virtual environment** (`.venv`) is a separate ledger for one project: its own Python packages, isolated from every other project.
The game's launcher already created one and installed everything. To use it in your own terminal, activate it first.

4.title: Calling Gemini
body: The `google-genai` SDK gives you a client object. You ask it to generate content for a model and read `.text` from the response.
4.code:
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(api_key=key)
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model=model, contents="Explain ROI in one line")
print(response.text)
4.note: Only create a client inside a function — never at import time — so importing your file never touches the network.

5.title: Dependency injection: plug in a test fixture
body: If your function builds its own client, tests can't avoid the network. Instead accept an optional `client` parameter. Real use passes nothing; tests pass a fake with the same shape.
It's like a dry run with a practice account: swap the pretend account in for the real one and you can rehearse the whole process without spending real money.

0.title: HTTP in one page
body: Web services talk with **HTTP**. A client sends a **request** (a method such as `GET`, plus a path like `/product/7`); the server sends back a **response** (a status code plus a body, usually JSON).
Think of it as ordering at a shop counter: every request names an action (method), says which item it is about (path) and may carry details (body).
0.code:
GET /product/SKU-7          ← request
200 OK                     ← response status
{"id": "SKU-7", "price": 19.99}   ← response body

5.prompt: With the route `/product/{product_id}`, a request to `/product/SKU-7` sets `product_id` to…
5.explain: The captured segment is passed as-is; with a str annotation it stays the string "SKU-7".

2.2.quest: Expose FastAPI app and POST /reviews. Validate name is nonempty and rating is between 0 and 5 inclusive. Return the validated name and rating with HTTP 201.

0.title: POST sends a body
body: `GET` reads. `POST` sends data in the request **body**, usually JSON, for the server to process or store.

1.title: Pydantic: a checkout form
body: A **Pydantic model** declares the fields you expect and their types. Data that doesn't fit is rejected before your code runs — like a checkout form that refuses an order with no customer name.
1.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Review(BaseModel):
    name: str
    rating: float

s = Review(name="A", rating=4)
print(s.rating)

2.title: Constraints with Field
body: `Field` adds rules: `min_length=1` rejects empty text; `ge` / `le` mean greater-or-equal / less-or-equal (inclusive bounds).
2.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Review(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1)
    rating: float = Field(ge=0, le=5)

3.prompt: With `rating: float = Field(ge=0, le=5)`, is `rating=5` accepted?
options: Yes — le means ≤, so 5 is allowed
3.explain: ge and le are inclusive. gt and lt would be exclusive.

4.title: Models as route inputs
body: Use the model as a parameter type and FastAPI reads the JSON body into it. Invalid bodies get an automatic **422** response — your function never runs.
4.note: status_code=201 (Created) in the decorator changes the success code from the default 200.

options: The function runs with an empty name
5.explain: min_length=1 rejects the empty name during validation, before your function is called.

2.3.quest: Implement store_sale(db_path, product, amount). Create sales(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product TEXT, amount REAL) if needed, insert using parameters, commit, and return total row count. Persist across calls.

0.title: A database in a file
body: **SQLite** is a full SQL database stored in a single file — built into Python, no server needed. Data survives after your program exits.
0.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")   # creates the file if needed

1.title: Tables define the schema
body: A table is like a spreadsheet with fixed, typed columns. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` makes it only the first time.
`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` gives each row an auto-numbered id.
1.code:
con.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sales (
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
        product TEXT,
        amount REAL
    )
""")

2.title: Insert with ? placeholders
body: Pass values separately using `?` placeholders. SQLite keeps data and instructions apart.
Building SQL with f-strings lets a malicious value like `x'); DROP TABLE sales;--` become part of the command — that's **SQL injection**. The verification test tries exactly this.
2.code:
product, amount = "Mug", 12.5
con.execute("INSERT INTO sales (product, amount) VALUES (?, ?)",
            (product, amount))

4.title: Reading back: SELECT
body: `SELECT` queries rows. `fetchone()` returns one row as a tuple; `fetchall()` returns a list of them. `COUNT(*)` counts rows.
4.code:
count = con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales").fetchone()[0]
print(count)

2.4.quest: Implement async fetch_exchange_rate(reader). Await reader() once and return {"rate": value}. Convert TimeoutError to FastAPI HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Rate service unavailable"). Let other exceptions propagate.

0.title: Exceptions are warning flags
body: When something goes wrong Python **raises** an exception that travels up until someone catches it. `try` / `except` catches it.
Catch only what you know how to handle. `except TimeoutError:` is precise; a bare `except:` swallows everything, including your own bugs.

1.title: Translate at the boundary
body: Inside a web service, a low-level fault should become a meaningful HTTP response. FastAPI's `HTTPException` does that: raise it and FastAPI sends that status code and detail.
1.code:
from fastapi import HTTPException

raise HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Rate service unavailable")
1.note: 503 means 'temporarily unavailable — try later'. It's the honest code when a dependency times out.

3.title: async and await
body: `async def` defines a **coroutine** — a function that can pause while waiting on slow I/O so other work can run. Inside it, `await` waits for another coroutine's result.
Calling an async function doesn't run it; it returns a coroutine object you must `await`.
3.code:
import asyncio

async def read_rate():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)    # pretend I/O
    return 3.3

async def main():
    v = await read_rate()
    print(v)

asyncio.run(main())

5.title: Putting it together
body: Await the slow call inside `try`, translate the one error you understand, and let everything else propagate so real bugs stay visible.

6.title: Your mission: fetch_exchange_rate
body: Write `async def fetch_exchange_rate(reader)`. Await `reader()` **once** and return `{"rate": value}`. If it raises `TimeoutError`, raise `HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Rate service unavailable")` instead. Any other exception should propagate unchanged.

0.title: Why split documents?
body: AI retrieval works on small, searchable pieces called **chunks** rather than one huge document. A question then matches the few chunks that matter.
Like splitting a long contract into short clauses: each clause is small enough to read and search on its own.

4.title: Cosine similarity
body: Divide the dot product by both norms: `dot(a, b) / (norm(a) * norm(b))`. The result depends only on direction.
`1` = same direction · `0` = perpendicular (unrelated) · `-1` = opposite. Scaling a vector doesn't change its score.
4.note: Like comparing two customers by what they tend to buy, ignoring how much each one spends overall.

2.title: Adding entries: upsert
body: Each entry has a string **id**, the **document** text and its **embedding**. `upsert` inserts new ids and overwrites existing ones, so running your code twice doesn't duplicate data.
2.code:
notes.upsert(
    ids=["0", "1"],
    documents=["Invoices are due in 30 days", "Refunds take 5 business days"],
    embeddings=[[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]],
)
2.note: Passing embeddings yourself means Chroma never downloads an embedding model.

4.title: Querying
body: `query` takes a **list** of query vectors and returns the nearest entries. Results are nested: one inner list per query.
4.output:
[['Invoices are due in 30 days', 'Refunds take 5 business days']]
['Invoices are due in 30 days', 'Refunds take 5 business days']

0.title: The agent loop
body: An **agent** repeats a cycle: the model **decides** what to do → your code **acts** (runs a tool) → the result is **observed** and added to history → repeat until the model gives a final answer.
It's like a manager's routine: check the dashboard, take an action, review the result, repeat.

1.title: History is memory
body: Each step appends a record so the next decision can see what happened.

It's like a franchise handbook: write it once and every branch runs the business the same way.
